header:
Date: 2025-07-21 15:00 PDT
Duration: 54m
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Kapoor (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ethan Park (BrightFrame VP Eng), Lina Zhou (BrightFrame ML Platform), Rajiv Menon (BrightFrame Security), Carly (Product), Alex (note-taker)
summary: Discovery for migrating BrightFrame's conversational assistant and batch embedding pipelines off their incumbent managed endpoint (OpenAI/Azure) to Redwood. Key concerns: eval parity (quality), latency at 99th percentile, cost predictability, private deployment options for PHI-adjacent workloads, and compatibility with vLLM/TGI-based self-hosted components. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run parity benchmarks, share pricing and dedicated configs, and schedule security deep-dive.
topics: hosting options (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intro — I'm Maya, AE here, and Diego from our SE team will jump into the technical bits.
[00:08] Ethan (BrightFrame): Hey thanks, Ethan here. We're mostly curious about migration options. We're on a managed endpoint today (OpenAI via Azure) and costs are creeping up.
[00:16] Diego (Redwood SE): Great. Can you walk us through what you're running today? Models, request patterns, any self-hosted tooling like vL L M —vLLM— or TGI?
[00:27] Lina (BrightFrame ML): Yeah, sorry, our pipeline is mixed. For chat we call OpenAI gpt-4-like endpoints, for embeddings we have a batch job on Azure functions. We also have an experimental in-house inference plane using v LLM and TGI for lower-cost offline jobs.
[00:43] Rajiv (Security): From my side we need to know about data residency, KMS integration, SAML SSO and audit logs. If we move away from OpenAI we need the same paper trail.
[00:52] Diego: Totally. Redwood Private supports bring-your-own KMS and audit logs; Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools. We can cover SOC2 compliance and SAML.
[01:03] Carly (Product): Eval parity is a big one. Our product team sees hallucination differences across models and even tokenization affects scoring. How do you verify parity?
[01:13] Maya: Good question. We run side-by-side evals with your test prompts and typical payloads. Diego will outline the parity benchmark approach.
[01:20] Diego: Right — we do a multi-axis comparison: quality metrics (exact match, BLEU-ish for outputs where applicable, human eval spot checks), throughput and latency at different sequence lengths, and cost per 1k tokens. For vLLM/TGI parity we usually convert checkpoints and run compatibility tests; sometimes small adaptor code is needed.
[01:36] Ethan: When you say "convert checkpoints" — we have some models hosted internally on TGI. Will Redwood accept those?
[01:42] Diego: In most cases yes. We often need model artifacts packaged in standard formats. For certain exotic optims we might need to adjust compilation flags. vLLM caches and KV cache handling can differ — we try to emulate the same decode steps to match outputs.
[01:56] Lina: Perf: our 99th pctl needs to be under 400ms for short chat turns, and embeddings batch jobs need to finish overnight — cost is sensitive there.
[02:06] Maya: Sounds reasonable. Our Dedicated offering can provide tail latency SLAs and predictable capacity; Hosted can be cheaper to start. For embeddings we recommend batching profiles with cache disabled for deterministic output.
[02:18] Ethan: What's the lift to move from OpenAI/Azure to Redwood Hosted? Is it mostly an API key swap?
[02:24] Diego: For simple gen it's often straightforward: prompt/response mapping and any streaming hooks. But differences come from tokenization, system prompt handling, and subtle temperature/sampling defaults. So we run a parity run to quantify delta.
[02:39] Rajiv: I want the legal angle — retention policies, deletion APIs, and if we can keep logs in our VPC. For PHI-adjacent data we might need Private/on-prem.
[02:49] Maya: We have Private deployments for high compliance needs and Dedicated for enterprise isolation. Both support customer-managed KMS and VPC peering.
[02:58] Carly: What's the typical migration timeline for a POC?
[03:01] Diego: Usually 2–6 weeks for a pilot: initial parity benchmark (1 week), set up Dedicated or Hosted env (1 week), integration and smoke tests (1–2 weeks), then a small shadow/pilot ramp. Private/on-prem adds provisioning time.
[03:18] Alex (note taker): (murmur)
[03:23] Maya: Any blockers on your side to start the parity run next week?
[03:26] Ethan: We need to extract our eval set and get legal to sign the NDA for infra access. Also, can you simulate our 95th/99th pctl load?
[03:36] Diego: Yes, we can replay traffic shape and run load tests to match pctl latency. Send us a representative sample payload and we can mirror it.
[03:43] Lina: One thing — some of our prompts rely on special tool-calling behavior. Does Redwood support function calling or structured outputs?
[03:51] Maya: Yes, we support function calling patterns and structured response schemas; we can map to your tool endpoints. There can be subtle differences in streaming chunking though — Diego will call that out.
[04:02] Diego: On streaming, chunk boundaries and partial tokens may differ; we recommend a short shim for deterministic parsing. Also note that quantization and kernel selection can change logits slightly and may alter beam ordering in edge cases.
[04:17] Ethan: Cost — our CFO wants predictable unit economics. How do Dedicated reserved pools compare to OpenAI's per-token?
[04:24] Maya: Dedicated is a reserved monthly commit with predictable throughput; unit cost depends on model size, quantization and batch profiles. We can model your current spend and show cost delta. Usually customers see lower per-token cost at scale.
[04:36] Rajiv: For compliance docs, can you provide SOC2 Type II report and encryption at rest details? Also, do logs include user-level IDs for auditing?
[04:46] Maya: Yes, SOC2 and encryption details; audit logs include request-level metadata. Private deployments can push logs to your SIEM.
[04:55] Carly: Any gotchas with vLLM/TGI compatibility?
[04:58] Diego: The big ones: tokenizer differences, custom operators in TGI, and cache semantics. For example we saw a customer where vLLM used a different eos handling and outputs diverged. We add a conversion step and run human spot checks.
[05:13] Ethan: If outputs differ, do you help with prompt re-tuning?
[05:16] Maya: Yes, our SEs help with prompt engineering and we can run A/Bs on rollout.
[05:20] Lina: We also need determinism for certain batch analytics; how deterministic are outputs across runs?
[05:25] Diego: Determinism depends on seeding and sampling. For deterministic needs we suggest greedy or beam with fixed seeds and consistent tokenizers; also disable GPU non-deterministic kernels. That can increase latency.
[05:38] Ethan: Ok. Pricing and the parity benchmark are the big artifacts we need.
[05:42] Maya: We'll send a starter parity plan and pricing models. Diego will schedule the bench.
[05:46] Rajiv: Last — we need a written migration rollback playbook. If something regresses in production how do we fail back to OpenAI?
[05:55] Diego: We recommend a traffic-router with canary rules and automatic fallback to your current provider. We can help template the runbook.
[06:03] Carly: Great. Thanks everyone.
[06:05] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with the doc bundle and next steps.
[06:10] (call ends)
